utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, I hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, you may sit down. Good morning, General Talic. Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic, you may or may not be informed that measures are underway to ensure that the situation which this Trial Chamber complained about with regard to legal representation last week be solved on a permanent basis. I know that as actually Ms. Fauveau stated last week that a request has been filed with the Registry, with the Registrar, so that Ms. Fauveau herself be assigned as co-counsel with Maitre de Roux in your defence. So we should have a confirmation of that at least on a temporary basis pending formal endorsement of it in a very short time. And that should be satisfactory for all of us. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much for your concern about my legal representation, and by the 20th, I will be able to inform you whether Mr. De Roux will be my counsel or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, General Talic, I have just been given a document which confirms that on Thursday, 14th February, I don't know if you believe in Valentine's day but this is the 14th of February, the Registry assigned Mademoiselle Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic as co-counsel to you. This is in accordance with Rule 16(C) of the directive on assignment of Defence counsel which stipulates that upon the request of lead counsel, the Registry may assign a co-counsel to the accused if it is in the interests of justice to do so. Mr. De Roux submitted a request to the Registry on February 13th, 2002, for the assignment of Mademoiselle Fauveau as co-counsel and in view of her legal experience and familiarity with the case, the Registry consented. With respect to the status of Maitre Michel Pitron, since he never submitted his curriculum vitae or qualifications to the Registry for review, he was never formally assigned as co-counsel. The Registry is currently considering whether to assign him as legal assistant. Should you have any further queries in relation to this matter, please let us know. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour once again thank you very much, I have no other questions and I fully agree with Ms. Fauveau acting as co-counsel in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had no doubt that you would agree to being represented by Ms. Fauveau, who is a very capable lawyer. Thank you General Talic, you may sit down. So I think we missed a formality, calling the case. Could you please call the case just for the formality of it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure this is not going to be a major cause for the annulment of proceedings later.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this morning Joanna Korner together with Ms. Anna Richterova who appears before Your Honours for the first time in this case and assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For General -- for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm John Ackerman, my co-counsel Milka Maglov has returned and Tania Radosavljevic is with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Ackerman. For General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic and I am representing General Talic in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Fauveau. So I sent word last Friday that I have an important engagement today at about 1.00 which I simply cannot miss and with your indulgence, I would like to finish before that to enable me to be in town around about 1.00, 1.15, so please, we will need to adjust our work schedule for today accordingly. I would suggest, unless you have something important to tell me beforehand, that we go through the various points that were raised during the informal meeting chaired by my senior legal officer a week and a half ago, go through the points that you discussed and see whether there is anything else to add, whether we need to formalise anything in that regard, okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour may I just mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It arises from the Status Conference but I wonder if I could deal with it out of order because Mr. Inayat is presently loitering outside court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a question of whether there is going to be any necessity to call him to deal with the exercise he's done now once, I think, of going through the documents. Your Honours may recall and have been given a copy of the schedule which -- needless to say I think that I have left behind, which -- in which Mr. Inayat went through the provenance or where the documents came from. The Defence put in a joint series of objections based on, I think, very much the same formula, namely the lack of seals, signatures and all the rest of it. And Your Honours will have seen, we discussed the matter during the informal conference with the Senior Legal Officer. If it's possible, it would seem to us that the sensible way of dealing with this, rather than going through this exercise each time, subject to Your Honours' agreeing to admit the Banja Luka documents with all the caveats that we discussed, in other words that Your Honours will be looking for indicia of reliability, authenticity, and what could happen is simply that the Defence would provide a document indicating to which exhibits they would invite Your Honours, certainly at some stage, to say that there is insufficient indicia of reliability and even though formally admitted Your Honours shouldn't act on them. It was discussed and I'm simply raising it now so to find out whether the Defence agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't hear anything different in what Ms. Korner is saying to you this morning from what we'd already agreed that when she submits the documents we provide our written objections where we are contesting the prima facie showing of indicia of reliability and it then is the burden of the Prosecutor, it's not our burden, to do anything after that point. It's the Prosecutor's burden to show that there are indicia of reliability with regard to the documents we've complained about, and it seems to me that the Prosecutor can't, under any circumstances, somehow shift the burden to us regarding their documents. I surely wouldn't try to do that with regard to documents I want to admit to make it her burden to somehow deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We believe that some of the documents do not have enough, sufficient probative value in order to be admitted into evidence. We refer to Article 89(C) regarding the probative value of the documents. We believe that the documents in question do not have probative value. There is a whole series of documents signed by a certain individual by the name of Milos whose identity we do not know. This person is not I'd identifiable and we consider these documents to be anonymous documents. But this Chamber decided on the 5th of February, this year, not to admit a document because it was an anonymous document and because the Defence could not proceed with the verification of the authenticity and the credibility of the documents. We believe that the documents signed by this individual by the name of Milos fall exactly in the same category. As regards documents without signatures, I know that the Chamber rendered a decision to that effect and I am following the guidelines governing the admissibility of the documents. Do I agree with the decision in question, however we must take into account that it is possible that some of these documents were not signed by the person who should have signed them, because that person was not agreeable with the contents of the document. So this document -- this kind of document could be admitted. However we have to consider it beforehand why the individual in the question did not sign these documents. There are also three documents which we contest because they are documents from 1993. However, these documents concern events that took place in 1993 but do not date from 1993. The indictment covers the period from 1 April to 31 December 1992 [As translated] and they do not fall consequently within the scope of the indictment. I must express my surprise and my concern that the Prosecutor wishes to tender these documents and have them admitted, documents concerning the events that took place in 1993. I think that the Prosecutor then deems these documents to be credible and with the sufficient probative value. But these events and these documents were cited by the Prosecutor in the indictment as events that took place in 1992. I have nothing against these three documents being admitted into evidence. However, I think that the Prosecutor should then withdraw the indictment in respect of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour excuse me there is apparently a problem with the translation. The transcript says that Ms. Fauveau said that these 1993 documents cover the period from 1st of April to 31 December, 1992. I'm reasonably certain that's not what she said. I think she said that they do not deal with that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour if it may assist, I did tell Defence counsel yesterday, I'm sorry not yesterday, whenever it was, that I was going to withdraw those. I don't know what the third document is. I've only spotted two. I'm very sorry, Your Honour it's entirely my fault I have left my document in my room and without my markings, I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I am used to doing the same thing. I don't know how many times a day. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour I do intend to and I will formally withdraw the two, I only noticed two documents from 1993. But I'm not quite clear from what Madam Fauveau says. Is the answer that she still wishes at this stage, because I'm going to ask Your Honours to admit the whole Banja Luka set of documents today minus the two we are going to withdraw. If she is still saying that she wishes there to be evidence given and for us to go through the documents because if so certainly we will do that and if Your Honours want that to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I just want to make sure that the record continues to show that it is my contention that documents should not be admitted without the Prosecutor being required to make at least something beyond a prima facie showing of reliability -- of authenticity. I think there should at least be a showing of authenticity that rises to a civil law standard, that of more probable than not. But I want to make sure that I'm not agreeing that a document may be admitted just because it has these prima facie evidences of authenticity. I think it needs to go way beyond. And that's my position that I will maintain throughout the case but I understand Your Honours have ruled and I will abide by that ruling even though I think the standard must be higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also think that the Prosecutor should demonstrate the prima facie credibility of the documents but I am not persuaded that testimony of Mr. Inayat is going to elucidate certain points. All he can say is where he found the documents or who it was who gave him the documents. That may be useful for two or three documents that were received by him in person. However, I don't think that it should work for other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But again, you are moving from the very restricted parameters that we indicated in our decision, into what then necessarily becomes more tangible evidence and more concrete evidence, regarding the credibility and the probative value, the relevance and the probative value of those documents. What we have to establish in the early stages is whether there are the preliminary, the indicia of credibility that we refer to in our decision and that's about it. As far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, as such, having seen the document that Mr. Inayat or the Prosecution prepared, in other words relative to each and every one of these documents with an indication as to provenance, for the purposes of the exercise, the initial exercise that we have to go through, I think it would be sufficient from the Chamber's point of view, if Mr. Inayat came here and confirmed that particular document. Then obviously, while he is in the witness box, he can be cross-examined by you with regard to particular documents, and that is perfectly regular. That is perfectly not just regular but the Trial Chamber is prepared to allow, but with regard to other documents that are not being seriously contested, I think we can move ahead, but please don't put questions to Mr. Inayat at this particular stage with regard to authenticity proper, because he may not, and probably he isn't, be the right person to answer those questions. As I already -- or rather as we promised you when we gave that decision, all the options regarding authenticity relevance and probative value related to each and every one of these documents will remain unprejudiced. The admission of these documents at this particular stage as exhibits does not in any way compromise the rights that you have under the Rules and under even basic rule -- principles of justice to contest each and every one of those documents later on, as has happened basically in practically all the cases that have taken place here in this Tribunal. So I think that should be clear. If it is desirable -- if you prefer to -- that we dispose of Mr. Inayat first, and call him so that he can go and continue with his other work, I think we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm entirely -- if Your Honours wish to -- I simply want to know whether he was going to be called at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think at this stage, Ms. Korner -- I mean the message is loud and clear, I think I would admit Mr. Inayat here in this trial, in this courtroom, he will go through this process which hopefully should be a short one. He will just confirm that document that he was provided the Trial Chamber with two weeks ago or -- either he or you, I don't remember. Any way. He will confirm it. And then if there are questions that the Defence teams would like to pout to him, he should be in a position to answer them and that should close the chapter for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful. As Your Honours may have seen, I was handed a package and I've now got the document that I marked up. Your Honours, the ones we propose to remove, and these are the only two I spotted and no doubt Madam Fauveau can assist, if Your Honours go to the schedule, to document P264, they have been premarked now -- Your Honours, I should tell Your Honours that we've given Your Honours a new one this morning because we've removed certain documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may think you gave us another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. We gave it to Your Honour's clerk, whatever, the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's different in that it doesn't contain Mr. Inayat's extra added bits but it's a new list because we have extracted some of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does the Prosecutor believe that we were supplied with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know. Did we supply them? All it does is it reflects the two documents I'm about to take out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I just think nothing should be supplied to the Trial Chamber without also being supplied would to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're definitely right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree and I'm sorry, and it will be supplied almost immediately. But Your Honours, if you look at the old list, the one that Mr. Inayat compiled, or rather that he added the source, if you go to P264, I'm sorry, I don't think the pages are numbered, they will be numbered in future but it's the 14th page, I numbered mine myself. You will see there a document that says, "A paper on festive days of the Serbian military." Which was given an approximate date of the 29th of June, 1992. It was objected to and it became clear when one read the content more carefully that it must have been published in 1995, because it refers to the 81st anniversary of the assassination of the Archduke in Sarajevo. So that one has been removed. The next document, is 357, P357. That document was a list of -- from a newspaper of destruction of cultural property but as Madam Fauveau says quite correctly, in 1993. And that has also been removed. Now, she mentioned a third document and I didn't spot it, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two other documents concerning 1993, P355 and 444. P355 concerns the events which took place in September, 1993, and P444 concerns the destruction of religious facilities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P355, it describes the JNA arming of the Serbs in 1992. That's why it's there. It's largely concerned, I agree with 1993 but there is a reference to that and that's clearly an important part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is the case, it will definitely be admitted on a prima facie basis because as I tried to explain last time there may be statements prior to 1992 or subsequent to 1992, which may be relevant because they throw a light on either on the events that happened in 1992 or on the former mentis of the accused or some of the allege accomplices Relevant to the period we are concerned with. So as far as that document, P355, definitely we will go ahead. It will be admitted with the same caveats as explained earlier. The other document, Ms. Fauveau, was? 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P444.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, document 444, -- would Your Honour, forgive me one moment while I just look at the actual document? Your Honour, I agree and we will remove that. I had missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that solves that problem. Let me make a note of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we will do is, because we premarked exhibits we are simply going to leave that exhibit number blank because otherwise we will get into terrible confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In those circumstances, I'll call Mr. Inayat without further ado.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you Ms. Korner. Please admit Mr. Inayat in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back to this courtroom. You are going to be asked to make the solemn declaration that you are familiar with and then you may sit down and some questions will be puts to you by the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, in respect of the documents which have been placed into the binders from the Banja Luka municipalities, were you asked to conduct the same exercise that you did in respect of Dr. Donia's documents?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I was asked, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that to check from the documentation available how the -- each document came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I did precisely. That I checked the source for each and every document listed in this exhibit list, Banja Luka exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is that recorded in the list which has been given to the Court and to Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That's correct, the last column I have added and there I have inserted the sources for the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just one other matter, then, Mr. Inayat. Were you also asked to do a check relating to the minutes or records which had been acquired of the assembly held by the association of Banja Luka municipalities later the Autonomous Region of Krajina assembly?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I was asked to conduct a search on those documents and I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this goes back sometime ago now to questions that were put to Dr. Donia about which assembly minutes he had been shown. And there seemed to be a suggestion that he'd only be shown some and others had been deliberately withheld so I just want to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to make it clear that that was not the suggestion at all, not that the Prosecutor was deliberately with holding but that he was getting a skewed view of what a went on because he did not have access to all of the documents. That was the point, not that the Prosecutor was doing something wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was the impression that this Trial Chamber got any way. I never had the impression given that anything irregular was being alleged to have been done by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, all I was concerned about, in other words, that it was not that the Prosecution had made a selective selection of the documents in its possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I never made such claim, nor do I do so now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful in that case I needn't trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had even made a statement when this came up, I don't remember whether it was you or Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Probably Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean it was very clear that it was made clear and accepted by my -- by the Defence that basically, Mr. Donia was -- had seen what was available at the time and that you definitely did not have more documents. Then at some later point in time, it transpired that you had one or two further documents, which Mr. Cayley, I think, brought forward and asked Mr. Donia about, so more or less, I mean, I don't think you need to trouble yourself with that point. There is no indication that should make the Trial Chamber worry about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful. In that case, that's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Inayat so you confirm the correctness of everything that is indicated on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have very conscientiously done this exercise in good faith and I believe that the sources that I've indicated in the last column are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman? Are there any questions that you would like to put to Mr. Inayat with regard to the list itself and to any particular item of documents that is referred to in that list? Or sources or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Ms. Fauveau is basically prepared to ask any questions with regard to this. I will have one question but I think she is prepared to go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Last time you said that you were personally present only in the building of the municipality of Banja Luka during the seizure in February 1998.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: In 1998, February of 1998, I was present in the Municipal Assembly building during the search and seizure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present in the centre of the Security Services in Banja Luka at a given moment?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I never visited the CSB building during the search and seizure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then, in fact, you wouldn't be able to explain to us how the seizure was carried out in the centre?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Although I was not present, but I have read through the reports prepared by the search officers and I have also gone through the search and seizure lists that are prepared at the time of material that is seized so I have a fair idea of what went on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka is in fact a police station?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's a regional police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all the documents that were seized in the Security Services Centre of Banja Luka -- are you sure that they were documents written in that centre? Or addressed to that centre?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Yes. Majority of the documents were either initiated in the regional police station or these were documents that were a result of a correspondence between the CSB and other organisations such as the police -- municipal police stations in the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, do you know if it also had documents that the Serbian police had seized when they were searching people or organs?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the documents that we seized also included documents that were sort of reports prepared by the local police forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was: The Serbian police, when they searched, made searches, did it also seize documents and objects possessed by persons? Were these documents and objects conserved in the security service centre in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I just ask for clarification, by Serbian police, do you mean from Serbia itself, not Bosnian Serb?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No I'm talking about the police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: For me to be able to answer this question, I really have to go back and look at the seized material, and if it pleases Your Honours, I can submit a declaration to this particular question indicating the answers that you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, this is exactly the problem that I'm referring to, because in my opinion, and I'm persuaded that this is the case, among these documents there are other documents that the Serbian police had seized elsewhere. This is why I say that I don't believe that Mr. Inayat can elucidate this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will come to it later. In the meantime, please proceed with any further questions that you may have. I personally doubt very much whether Mr. Inayat is the right person to answer that in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could have you a look at document number P207? That id the Document that you received from the AID agency in Sanski Most, investigations and documentation agency in Sanski Most. The person who gave you this document, did he explain to you how this agency got hold of this document?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I personally received in August of 1999 from AID Sanski Most. Normally when investigators receive these documents we exchange receipts. We give them a receipt that we have received the document and they also note that down, that on this particular day, these documents were given but we don't go into the details because these have to be brought back and reviewed so, yes, I'm afraid, he didn't tell me how he received this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So the other people who received -- other people who received the document by -- from the agency, from the AID agency or the Ministry of the Interior or from the liaison officer in Bosnia and Herzegovina, they also don't know how these documents arrived in the possession of the Bosnian organs?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: No, that is not true. Documents that were received in 1996, in November, 1995, and in April, 1996, in Bihac, there it was made very clear where the documents had been seized from and I think in my earlier testimony, I had pointed that out, that the areas from where these documents had been seized in Bihac, in Sanski Most, in Kljuc, in Petrovac and in Krupa, the staff members of the Office of the Prosecutor visited those areas and they received information also in writing as to when this collection was seized by the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we say the same thing for the document that the AID agency in Bugojno forwarded for the document that the Ministry of the Interior transmitted and for the document that the liaison officer in Bosnia and Herzegovina transmitted?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I think that's a fair assessment that most of these documents that had been given to us had actually been seized early on in 1995 and 1996 and they have been given to us in small collections during these last several years, but most of these documents do come from their seizures that happened in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But among some of these documents, there are documents for which you don't know how they came into the possession of the organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: They would be such documents that I'm personally not aware of but I can go back and ask my colleagues who had received these documents to give me an answer and I can submit that declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible for the Prosecutor's Office to give us information, a report, on all the documents that were seized or that were transmitted rather by any agency in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to tell us how these organs in Bosnia and Herzegovina came into possession of these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think I will allow to you answer that question, Mr. Inayat. You do not -- he can not be asked to give commitments on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. Your question is being directed to the Office of the Prosecutor and I wouldn't even allow Ms. Korner to give you a definitive reply on that this morning, definitely not. I think you should go on to your next question, but don't expect the witness to answer that question. You may eventually plead on that. Your request may be taken into consideration by the Prosecution in assessing whether their case will be stronger or weaker if they do what you request or they don't do, they don't come forward with what you like. I think I would go to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was quite technical. I'm not asking whether they are going to give it to us or not but whether this is a possibility, whether it is possible to indicate to us how a document arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... asked to answer that question. You then make a specific request to the Prosecution in the sense that you make a submission that you think that the Prosecution ought to bring forward this particular piece of evidence and we will consider it, but not from Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we are requested to explain how a particular document arrived in the Office of the Prosecutor, then we will do our best to find out. We can't possibly give a global answer as to how every document in this institution arrived here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is even a step further than that. Because what Madam Fauveau is requesting is for the OTP to bring forward an explanation or a confirmation as to how suppliers of information to Mr. Inayat or to the Office of the Prosecutor obtained the information in the first place, so this is why I'm definitely not going to expect or allow Mr. Inayat to give that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say that some cases we might be able to answer that question. In others, not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions but I would appreciate it if the Prosecutor could provide us with the information on how the documents from Republika Srpska were -- came into the possession of the organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In our idea, in our opinion, these documents are ones the authenticity of which will always remain suspect. Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska were at war. We can't quite simply accept documents without a signature, without a seal, without all the other attributes that a document has to have and which come from a party which is an enemy party in the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, that is a question of the reliability of those documents and the probative value of -- apart from relevance, the probative value of those documents when we come to that stage. Obviously this is going to be weighted in due course together with other evidence. Don't be surprised if you get a very simple explanation to your request. These things happen. I can assure you that they happen. Any further -- yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, would you tell us what the AID organisation was before it acquired the name AID?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: My understanding is that the SDB or the state security service was transformed into AID in -- sometime in the beginning of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was the state security service of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Many of whom would have been members of and supporters of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. In any event they were part of the government headed by Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you -- you got these documents from a number of sources and you went through those sources with the Trial Chamber the first day you appeared as a witness. Do you have an opinion, a sense, of which source from which you received documents you consider the most reliable source and which you would consider the least reliable and do you think it might be helpful for you to advise the Trial Chamber of that to assist them in their efforts to determine the reliability of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't like objecting but I do object to that question. I don't think this is a proper question to ask the investigator. It's a matter for Your Honours to decide having heard the evidence, all the evidence, around the documents, what in your opinion should be reliable and attract more weight than other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is sustained. Perhaps Mr. Ackerman, you would like to rephrase your question in a sense of asking the witness whether there are any documents that he has reason to doubt himself as to their reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually that's exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you're prepared to put that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I do. That's the question I was going to ask next.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the thousands and thousands of documents you've received, I suspect you have run across some that you believe were not authentic?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't sit here and say that I have reviewed each and every document. The documents that have been relevant to this particular case, I have seen those documents, I have tried to find the sources for those documents, and it's very difficult for me to point out a document which I believe was not authentic. I haven't come across any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are aware, are you not, that there are -- that efforts have been made in the past and perhaps continue to be made, to create false documents and plant false documents regarding events that occurred during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Personally I'm not aware of any such false documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you were not -- you're not aware of and were not listening to the testimony of the last witness that testified here regarding that issue? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: When you say the last witness, you mean Mr. Muharem Krzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I did listen to parts of his testimony but I didn't listen to the whole thing so I must have missed this particular bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't see the part where he claimed that a document that I had showed him must have been manufactured by the Security Service of Republika Srpska and that he claimed that it was not a genuine document?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't listen to that particular part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Do Your Honours have any questions of Mr. Inayat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one question to Mr. Inayat

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: During this whole exercise, Mr. Inayat, were there any documents that in your conscience and in your better judgement told you to discard and you discarded?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was provided a list of documents by the trial attorneys that were going to be used as exhibits and waist told to go through each and every document, which I did to find out the sources, and I did not recommend any document to the trial attorneys on the ground that I believed that document to be not authentic or a fake document. I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a follow up to your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, I take it you would not have the authority to throw out a document because you think it's not authentic? You couldn't just throw it in the trash can, could you?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: No, we work as a team and as team leader, I enjoy a lot of respect from the attorneys and if in my opinion, there had been something in a document that would have attracted my attention and to point that out, I would have certainly done that and I'm sure that there would have been a discussion on it but I didn't come across any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You came across all of those documents that were apparently signed by a person named Milos, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have no idea who that person is, do you?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: But the exercise I was conducting primarily was to find out the sources and I knew that this particular documentation where Milos has signed came from the Banja Luka services -- the regional police station so it was seized so I knew that it was authentic because members of the Office of the Prosecutor had personally seized those documents so they didn't seem fake to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yeah, but as far as you know, those could very well be documents that were sent there by some nut who was making everything up and they just filed them among their papers there, it doesn't -- just the fact that they were there doesn't mean that they were accurate, does it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, Mr. Inayat. How can he tell you yes or no? He doesn't know. It was not part of his job. Yes, Ms. Korner do you need your witness any further?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, I think you can withdraw. You have been most helpful as on previous occasions. The Trial Chamber would like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then Your Honours, I would ask that the documents shown on this index be formally admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have filed our objections but I just want to draw your attention, Your Honour, to these Milos documents. The Prosecutor is absolutely incapable of telling you who Milos is, absolutely incapable of providing us any information that would assist us in making that determination as to whether he was any kind of reliable source. These are simply anonymous documents, anonymous in the sense that Milos may not even be the name of the person who was authoring them, they are just signed with the name Milos. They were apparently sent off to the police station as some kind of reports to the police station, at least that's where they were found, but just because they were found there gives them no indicia of reliability whatsoever. Any nut can send any kind after letter any kind of a document that he or she wants to off to anybody he wants to send it to. People generally file those kinds of things among their records. But that doesn't give them any kind of reliability. And it seems to me that the Prosecutor has to go -- I mean that is not prima facie that it was found in the police station. The Prosecutor has to go somewhat beyond that and show to you that -- who the person was that authored these documents that say Milos so you will have some basis at least to make a determination as to whether the information contained in those documents has any kind of reliability at all. It's just an anonymous piece of paper with a name at the bottom of it and that's all it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we'll see as we go through those documents that Milos is not some nut sending unasked for reports. We are going to be suggesting that when you look at all the reports and the nature of those reports, that Milos was an operative, this is not the police station, this is the state security section of the CSB, and Your Honours, we will be asking Your Honours to look for other evidence which supports what is contained in those reports. In many senses, I'm somewhat surprised by the objection because there is a great deal about the Muslim extremists who are said to be attacking so -- but, Your Honour, that is what we will be suggesting Your Honours can find. But again it's a matter of at the end of the day, what weight do you attach to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. I think at this point in time, Mr. Ackerman. The way we should move further is as follows: I think point number 1 that should be made is the source, the origin or the alleged source or origin of these documents. I haven't is seen these documents as of yet. Obviously we will have to go through them like every other document as we go along, but I think point 1 that needs to be made by the Prosecution and which has been made is that these documents originate from the office of the security services or security -- any way, the secret service offices. That's number 1. If that is so, and if these are security, secret service documents, I'm not surprised at all that they can be anonymous or that they can have a name which to all intents and purposes cannot be attributed to any particular person, to any person in particular. These -- I mean, I personally have no experience with secret services but I know enough, however, not to be surprised at all that such a practice is adopted within secret service organisations and secret services. I think we will have to leave it unprejudiced for the time being. They will have to be admitted like all the other documents. Then obviously, as we go along, they will be put in juxtaposition that position with other documents originating from the same source and on that basis the Trial Chamber will be in a better position to form a judgement. But in reality what we are talking about and what we should be concerned and worried about is the ultimate relevance and probative value of those documents. I can assure you, Mr. Ackerman, that the three judges you have in front of you here will certainly not be -- will not be prepared to accept as having probative value documents they themselves have serious doubts about. I can assure you of this. But as at the present moment, I cannot exclude. I mean, I would first and foremost like to see them and secondly, also as we go along put them in juxtaposition with other documents that are forthcoming from the same source. For example, if other documents forthcoming from the same source have got their paternity black and white, while these haven't, I will obviously be asking ourselves why should these documents be different, whether this could be attributed to some sort of manoeuvring inside or outside the secret service, I have to wait. We will have to wait. And I will see. But we have certainly taken -- we will be taking into consideration your submission. For the time being, I think they have to be admitted. So these documents forming what we will be referring to the Banja Luka documentation are being admitted and I understand, Madam Registrar, that they will be given the same exhibit number that has been indicated to you by the Prosecution already following that sequence. Okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So shall we now go on to visit the various points that you discussed during the informal - I was told not to refer to it as a Status Conference - informal conference that we agreed you will be -- we will be holding from time to time? Especially as we approach a new municipality? Yes, Ms. Korner, I see you standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your honour, I was merely standing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down and I will do some talking first. I think the first point that was made according to the report that we have, the first point that was made precisely deals with the admission of documents in the records as exhibits, and what I have written here is that the Defence understands that the Trial Chamber will admit documents provided there is sufficient indicia of reliability but will keep stating their objections relating to stamps, signatures, et cetera for the record. None of the parties believe it is necessary to call the OTP investigator, Mr. Inayat each time to verify the list showing the sources of all the documents. Consequently, the Trial Chamber should decide whether it will endorse the agreement reached by the parties or whether it will continue to insist that Mr. Inayat be called to give evidence each time. If it decides to dispense with calling Mr. Inayat as a general rule, it may, of course, in any given instance ask the Prosecution to provide further evidence if they are not satisfied that there is sufficient indicia of reliability for this document. I think taking into consideration what has been written by the Senior Legal Officer and what went on this morning, I think you should be happy as we are, that the situation or the position is more or less clarified with regard to the admission of documents, and that we can proceed in future along the lines that have been adopted, at least up to this morning. Is that agreeable, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, subject to what I stated this morning about my continuing objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously. And Ms. Korner, I suppose hasn't got reason to object to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that goes in the records as point one on which there is an agreement. The next point was briefly raised last time and more or less I think we will -- we won't need to discuss it any further this morning except that I would like to remind you that with regard to the evidence of the particular deceased [Reatime transcript read in error "diseased"] witness that -- to whom reference was made sometime back, there seems to be an agreement between the Prosecution and the Defence that you will wait until colonel -- can I mention his name or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he's dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Until Colonel Selak gives evidence before oral argument on the issue of the admission of the evidence of the dead witness is dealt with. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you said "deceased," the transcript says "diseased."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, deceased but he probably was -- any way, are we agreed on this? So we will come to that later on and you tell me when it is convenient for you to deal with the matter. In the meantime, I would like you, particularly the Defence team for General Talic, to be prepared on this issue because more or less the objection was more from your side than from Mr. Ackerman's side. Then we have the problem of the 92 bis statement and more or less also we have clarified a part of this not during the last sitting but I think in the preceding one. It was agreed that in future the following procedure would be implemented for each new batch of Rule 92 bis statements: Prosecution will give advance notice to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber of the statements they intend to tender by way of Rule 92 bis for each municipality. That would be the first stage. The Prosecution will also provide copies of the statements to both the Chamber and the Defence teams of the Rule 92 bis statements in the form it intends to tender the statement. That is any deletions the Prosecutor wishes to make to the statement must be indicated to both the Defence teams and to the Trial Chamber. The Defence then would only object if they believe that the Rule 92 bis statement does not comply with the terms of the Rule itself. Otherwise, the Defence will simply advise the Trial Chamber if they want to cross-examine the witness or whether they request that the witness be brought forward for the purposes of being cross-examined. Let me stop here for the moment. Is this in conformity with what you discussed during that meeting? And do you agree that this should be the practice that will be followed by this Trial Chamber in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner -- Madam Fauveau, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, but two matters weren't clarified at the informal meeting. If Your Honours look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 16 of the note, it is still to do with the Rule 92 statements, unless Your Honour was carrying on to deal with further aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to deal with the next aspects relating to the 92 bis actually. Then I understand that the Prosecution raised the question of how Rule 92 bis statements that are admitted will be dealt with. In particular, it was asked whether they do -- whether they receive or ought to receive an exhibit number or whether they have to be read on to the record. The tendency, in the course of the meeting that you had, seems to have been, at least according to the Senior Legal Officer, that it should be clear that the statements do not have to be read on to the record. My tendency - and I haven't consulted my other two Judges on this, but I think it's pretty obvious - my tendency is to say that I would agree that they need not be read on to the records. Do you agree that they ought not or they need not be read on to the records? Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honour, there is no reason for doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My only caveat about that is that with regard to the transcripts of prior testimony that have not been furnished in translation form, if they are not read into the record, the accused will never know what the evidence against them is. And so I would suggest that they be provided in translation form and then they would not need to be read into the record. If they are not so provided, then I think they probably do need to be because these accused are entitled to know the evidence against them and to be able to advise counsel regarding that evidence. So I think one of the two things have to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is very sensible and very reasonable. Ms. Korner, what do you have to state about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we went through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it may have been the first Status Conference in front of Your Honour. They can't be translated because of the translation backlog. They are -- they are quite lengthy. The tapes of the -- what was said in the Bosnian language were provided to the Defence, and as I understood it, each of the accused was given an opportunity to listen to the tapes. What we can do is if we are going to mark them as exhibits, is we can put in - unless I'm corrected by anybody on my team - we can put in the transcript or such portion as we think is relevant, because a lot of it may not be relevant, and together put the tape that we have obtained of the original testimony in the Bosnian language, so that both will be on the record. But reading those transcripts into the record - if Your Honour says we ought, then we will, but it's a major effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will lead us into a never-ending alley. However, I do see the point raised by Mr. Ackerman. My suggestion to you is as follows: I think that as a matter of principle, we should first and foremost pay particular attention to the rule that the accused should always be in a position to understand in their own language each and every piece of evidence that is -- that the Prosecution intends to make use of in the case against them. So that is principle number one by which we have to abide. I think there is understanding, mutual understanding here, it's no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. question about it that there are problems related to possible translation of these documents, which -- to which we have to find a solution. One solution that was proposed and resorted to before was, as you correctly stated, you provided the Defence with the tape recording of the evidence or of the statements. Now, saying that you could indicate which parts from that previous testimony you would be making use of, or which parts from that statement the Defence ought to pay attention to, I think won't work. I think your duty is to provide the tapes. Your duty is also to indicate to the Defence which parts you will be referring to, but then it's up to Defence -- to the Defence, having already in their possession the version in English or in French, to advise their clients as to what they should concentrate upon. Leave it up to them, not up to you. I think the important thing is that you provide the tape recording of the totality of the statement. Then it's up to the Defence on how best to deal with that. However, while we are at this, I would like, because it is my fault, I never tried to verify this with the two accused. When this was resorted to on a previous occasion at the beginning of this trial, and supposedly we were told that you were going to be handed tape recordings of the evidence given by, I forgot who, Dr. Donia, I think or -- I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it was Dr. Donia's previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we made it clear that, of course, the utility of that depended very much on whether you would have the facility of using a tape recorder in -- where you are staying, in order to listen to those recordings. Was this made available? Did you have a tape recorder made available to you? Mr. Brdjanin? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you were afforded all the facilities in order to be able to listen to these tapes? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just telling you because it's our duty, I'm just telling you if at any moment you find difficulties in this -- in this aspect, in this regard, please inform the Trial Chamber through your legal counsel, through your lawyers, immediately. Because the Trial Chamber has a duty to ensure that you are given every opportunity to make it possible for you to defend yourself in the best way possible. Okay? And the same, I don't need to explain this to Mr. Ackerman or to Madam Fauveau. I'm sure that you will liaise with your clients on this as you go along. So there is agreement that provided this procedure is more or less followed, and followed to a satisfactory level, then statements -- there is no need for these -- such statements to be read on to the record. In other words, they will simply form part of the body of evidence that will eventually be read and considered by the Trial Chamber in the course of its deliberations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On this matter of providing tape recordings to the accused so that they can listen to this testimony that's going to be part of a 92 bis offering, there is a question of timing that I think is quite important. The Prosecutor must provide, it seems to me, those recordings on a timely basis, in the sense that once my accused has listened to that tape, it may very well be that he will then instruct me regarding matters that would prompt me to suggest to the Tribunal that that person needs to be brought here for cross-examination, where I had not thought that previously, and so this can't happen after the fact but it has to happen, I think, rather quickly, and I think perhaps at the beginning of each section, when the Prosecutor provides the list of 92 bis that are going to be contained within, say, the Sanski Most section, which is coming up next, that the tapes ought to be provided at that time, so that when we make the determination regarding whether or not we have objections to 92 bis at the same time, we will have been able to take instructions from our accused regarding whether or not we want to bring the witness for cross-examination, to the extent that might play upon that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that the Prosecution has not been cooperative along -- in that regard. I mean, with regard to 92 bis statements, for example, I mean, much of the work was done before we even appeared on the scene. And I think it was good work what was done. I mean it's -- yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say I appreciate that the tapes for the witnesses that Your Honours have agreed may be Rule 92 will be supplied to the Defence by the end of this week so that should give ample time, and we will try and do that in each case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. There is a question of what is being referred to as we need to agree on a procedure for marking the statements. To be frank with you, I have tried to understand where the difficulty lies, if there is a difficulty, and I personally can't see it. What I am told here is -- I have had some discussions with the registry and I'm informed that the statements would simply be given an exhibit number along with all the other exhibits admitted. If the Trial Chamber agrees with this procedure, we will then need to arrange for the statement of Witness 7.118, which the Trial Chamber has already accepted, pursuant to Rule 92 bis statement dated 30th January, 2002, to be produced by the Prosecution in its corrected form pursuant to the Rule 92 bis decision. Various parts of the statement were to be deleted, and then given an exhibit number. Is this agreeable to you or not? Because to me, it presents no difficulty at all. But there may be something that you discussed which I am missing completely. I mean, what -- what was the difficulty?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there is a disagreement among Trial Chambers that's been going on here for all the time that I've been here with regard to this issue, and different Trial Chambers have resolved it differently. Many Trial Chambers take the position, which would be the -- I call it, I guess, the classic common law position, that they ought not to ever see the statement of a witness unless something in the statement is called into question or it is used to the point where it makes sense that it become an exhibit, but many Trial Chambers will not look at statements of witnesses before those witnesses testify, or perhaps even not after they testify, because the testimony is supposed to be live testimony coming from the witness stand. That's the way some Trial Chambers view it. This Trial Chamber apparently has decided that it wants to look at these witness statements before each witness testifies. And I haven't objected to that because I recognise who you are and the approach you're taking to this case. So if that is going to be the case, then it seems to me that they don't need to become part of the evidence, they don't need to be marked in any way, they are simply being used by you as some kind of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not referring -- sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Ackerman, I'm not referring to those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Completely not. I am referring to statements regarding which there is a formal motion for admission in terms of 92 bis statements. For example, let's put it this week, there are going to be two witnesses, number 1 and number 2, whoever they are. There was no request with regard to any of these witnesses to have their statements admitted under 92 bis. I personally have adopted the system that before a witness comes along, I would rather prefer to know what kind of statements he or she has made in the past, because I am in a position to control better the evidence that the witness will be giving and the questions that you will be firing both from the Prosecution and from the Defence but obviously, I mean, I will not confront that witness with the statements that I would have read in the quiet of my own apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I misunderstood where we were and, in fact, somebody just called me to try to tell me to pay closer attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's stick to 92 bis. The question of numbering, this is what baffled me a little bit, if I am not -- if I am missing something because I frankly could not understand why there should be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't think there is a problem. The -- I think the only slight problem was the question of whether the statement that was actually certified under 92 is in fact the one that was translated into the Bosnian language. And I think there was a question of whether it was the English version or the actual certified one that needed to be exhibited. And therefore, what I suggest is that we exhibit both in the same way as we've been exhibiting the other documents, namely that the English version, which was not signed by them, will be Exhibit whatever A and the actual Bosnian statement which was acknowledged by them in the presence of the presiding officer will be B. And unless anybody sees any problem with that, that seems to me a simple solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't see any problem from our side, so if that is agreeable to the Defence, we can move along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I realise Mr. Ackerman was slightly at cross-purposes but I was going to say only in the circumstances where effectively there has been so much cross-examination on a witness statement, we would then apply to make that particular witness statement of a normal witness, for example, Mr. Krzic, who was here last week, an exhibit. But it would be not the rule but the exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While -- since Mr. Ackerman went astray for a while and referred to a practice that I have adopted for my own purposes, more than anything else, let me, however, explain to you the utility of it. We are still in the very early stages of this trial and as you may have noticed, I have not, neither personally nor as a team, decided that it's time to take an initiative in trying to thin and restrict the questions that you will be putting to the various witnesses that will come along. The advantage that I see in knowing beforehand what facts that particular witness can reveal in giving evidence will also help us to decide that we can ask the witness not to give information on certain facts on which the Trial Chamber is already satisfied that it doesn't need additional witnesses to come forward to give evidence upon. For example, I don't want to give an example with particular reference to a particular fact, but if there is a fact that has been stated by Dr. Donia, by Mr. Krzic, by the next witness, by the next witness, by the next witness, which is a fact which in itself is harmless, is neutral, in other words, it's not going to establish a responsibility on the part of any of the accused, then frankly, I do not see why the same question has to be repeated to the next witness so that we have a reaffirmation of a fact that has already been affirmed by many witnesses before. But this will take time. In other words, we are still in an early stage in this trial and knowing what a witness is likely to state in the witness box when he or she is -- comes forward as a witness, is called as a witness, helps to more or less regulate the proceedings in a more efficient fashion, in a more efficient way. But we will come to this later on and this is also part of another aspect that you discussed during the conference. There is an important point with regard -- and I finish with this now, with regard to 92 bis statement. I am just going to put it to you as it was put to me and I think there is an easy remedy to it. Again, the Trial Chamber needs to agree on a system for dealing with a particular issue. It refers to witness 7.118 who now wants protective measures and the Prosecution, as a result of that, wishes to know whether the previous statement testimony of this particular witness should remain under seal until after any identifying material is taken out. It's suggested that when the Prosecution submits a Rule 92 bis statement for admission, it should simultaneously make a request for protective measures it considers necessary. Any protective measures could then be put in place prior to the statement being marked as an exhibit. The Prosecution should be asked to clarify what protective measures they are seeking in relation to the statement of witness 7.118 which has already been accepted by the Trial Chamber but not formally produced in court or marked as an exhibit. I would leave you with this as food for thought while you have your coffee. We will resume in 20 minutes, 25 minutes time, and perhaps you can make the life of this Trial Chamber easier by providing us with a ready-made solution to this problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. We are anxious to hear the good news, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can't give you the good news about the witness because we haven't yet managed -- he told us he required protective measures and gave us a reason. We want to clarify some detail about that reason but we haven't contacted him because we were waiting until we had a ruling how somebody who wanted protective measures would be dealt with so that we could explain that to him. As far as that's concerned, in the future, subject to a witness having already made it clear that he wishes protective measures, when we file the request for Rule 92, we will file at the same time the request for protective measures. In fact, with this witness, it did arise after we'd already filed and we are still trying to clarify that with him. Your Honour, the only other aspect on that is this: If protective measures have been requested, and granted by Your Honours when granting the request for Rule 92, can we take it that the statement will not be released to public until identifying information has been redacted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think actually that my point of view would be as follows: Number one is that when you seek to file or to admit statements under 92 bis, you have several unknown facts, incognito, okay? Number one is whether the Defence is going to object. You also don't know if the witness will actually be seeking protective measures. It doesn't mean to say that a witness that had not sought protective measures on a previous occasion when he gave evidence will not want to seek protective measures now. And you may be actually taken by surprise at the very last moment, when the document would have formally already and admitted so we do have those incognita and also the related problems. What I suggest we do is this. That basing yourselves on these -- these possibilities, I think the safest way to approach this question would be to have them remain under seal until one, you know whether there is need for a redaction. That's number one, because it's not acceptable to have them readily available for anyone to read and then the ball of contention is paragraphs here and paragraphs there and they will redacted for all intents and purposes where you would have reached one aim but lost a lot in the course of that. And secondly, you never know whether there is going to be the need for protective measures. So what I will suggest is that once you know whether -- until you know whether there is an objection forthcoming from the Defence, whether there is a need for the statement to be redacted, and until you have reason to -- until you don't have -- until you have reason to doubt whether there will be the need for protective measures or not, these documents will remain under seal and the moment there is no need for redaction and/or the moment you know, because you have been given an indication on a prima facie basis at least that there is not going to be the need for protective measures, then those documents will remain under seal. After that, they will not remain under seal obviously. I think that is what I would like to suggest to you. I don't know if it is acceptable but I think it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does make sense and if, Your Honour, subject to the Defence's objections, says the statement will be admitted under 92 bis, and that protective measures are needed, then the statement will be redacted before it is released into general --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's the way we should proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only thing I'm not clear of, that's because I'm not 100 per cent familiar with the procedure as yet, is whether we do the redactions or it's done by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there have been both instances. I think there have been instances where you did the redaction yourselves before even asking for that statement to be admitted under 92 bis and there have been decisions by this Tribunal, admitting subject to a redaction taking place, in which case normally it's done by the Registry or by you taking up on the decision. But that is -- the important thing for this Tribunal is that the redaction takes place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think the Registry is responsible for it only when there is a decision to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sure that's a matter of technicalities which we can work out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the practice ought to be adopted whereby until the situation more or less clarifies, is clear, or crystallises as to whether there is need for redaction or whether there is going to be need for protective witnesses, those documents pending admission will remain under seal. Is that agreeable to you, Mr. Ackerman? Madam Fauveau? Okay. So we have cleared that up. Witness lists. I have highlighted here, Mr. Cayley pointed out that if the Trial Chamber takes a relatively strict approach to the question of hearsay evidence the Prosecution will be compelled to bring more eye witnesses for each incident. I think Mr. Cayley may have not understood me correctly or again, to put it mildly, I may not have myself made myself clear. What was I trying to tell you? And I will say it for the last time. I will not repeat it again. I, as a Trial Chamber, we do not intend to introduce new principles with regard to hearsay. Hearsay evidence, the Rule regarding the practice of this Tribunal, with regard to hearsay evidence is and will remain as it has been decided and as outlined by this Trial Chamber in its decision which you now have in written form. However, please, may I again remind you, that in front of you, you have not a lay jury that is going to decide on the facts of the case, but you have three professional Judges with all that it entails. That is number one.
