In other words, my message to you is if you lawyers think that this particular document, being a hearsay document, ought to receive much more attention than the Trial Chamber will eventually be prepared to give to it when it comes to probative value, please don't waste time. The idea is this: There was a question with regard to one particular document, not with regard to a lot of hearsay evidence that we have heard since the beginning of this trial. Why did this Trial Chamber find objection to that particular document? Because in reality, each piece of evidence within the parameters of the practice of this Trial Chamber regarding hearsay evidence should be read and construed parallel with, and as a corollary of the other principle that each one of you is bound by law to bring forward the best evidence. Now, there are cases where the best evidence is not available. There are cases where, according to the practice of this Tribunal, evidence which would otherwise under a common law regime amount to pure hearsay evidence and sometimes be excluded, will, under the practice of this Tribunal be admitted but don't get carried away with the idea that the practice of this Tribunal, of this Tri -- not this Trial Chamber, gives you a licence to dispense of what would otherwise be necessary to prove a particular fact. That particular document that we had objection with, this Trial Chamber has absolutely no objection with that particular document being admitted in evidence as being truly a document that was handed to Mr. Krzic by a number of persons. Now, that particular document, which is unsigned, intentionally unsigned, it is -- it was meant to be anonymous and it is presented as an anonymous document. In it, it purports to give to Mr. Krzic a lot of information on certain events, events that may form part of one or more of the various counts in the indictment against the two accused, and may -- specifically or even generally. Obviously if Mr. Krzic is in a position to state, "I verified these events mentioned in this document, and I can state that I had further information that those events actually took place," you will immediately realise the importance of having that document admitted because it will be looked at by this Trial Chamber in relation to the further statement made by Mr. Krzic. However, if the intention or the purpose of introducing that particular document is to prove that those events actually took place, and you don't have any further evidence to prove that those events actually took place, then you're going to face a brick wall, then you're going to have problems, because this Trial Chamber will certainly not be prone to accept, to convict anyone on the basis of mere hearsay evidence even though the practice of this Tribunal has been in the past and it will continue to do so, to admit hearsay evidence. I invite you to read again, and not just read the citation that we quoted if I remember well, from either Celebici or from the Delalic judgement, I think from the Celebici judgement, in our decision not just read the words but also read between the lines, the ultimate conclusion is don't ever expect hearsay evidence to be put in the same basket as all other evidence and given the same importance as all other evidence if, on the face of it, it does not warrant that much attention or that much value being attributed to it. There is also a very specific reference in the citation that we referred to to striking a balance between this relaxation of the Rule of hearsay evidence for the purposes of proceedings before this international Tribunal, in other words admission of hearsay evidence, and striking a balance between that and the rights of the accused. In other words, if the practice will resort itself through a situation obtaining whereby the accused, and for that purpose also the Prosecution, being faced with a situation of impotence with regard to some particular item of evidence brought forward by way of hearsay, reason being the impossibility to cross-examine a particular witness, or to contest the value, the face value, of that hearsay evidence, then the Trial Chamber might well find itself in a position where it has to protect either the rights of the accused or the rights of the Prosecution as the case may be, because what applies at this juncture to the Prosecution will eventually apply to the Defence, if you try to bring forward evidence which is strictly hearsay evidence. It will be admitted like we admit evidence, hearsay evidence when it is brought forward by the Prosecution, but please don't get carried away with the idea that this is a licence to make it possible for you to do away with the obligation that you have to bring forward the best evidence and rest -- be content with hearsay evidence as being the best you can do in the circumstances, if that is not the best that you can do in the circumstances. I also made it clear at that point that any document that we might exclude temporarily or for the time being because we consider that it will deprive the other party from due procedural rights, might be readmitted later on as well, just as much as it is perfectly possible that any document that we may be admitting with or without prejudice, we eventually will discard as of being completely of no value without removing it from the records. I think we have more or less made the situation as clear as can be. There is no strict rule like there is in common law jurisdictions. We will admit hearsay evidence but please do keep in mind that we are three judges and when we say, "Let's move forward, don't give this document as much attention as you would like to," it's because we see that eventually we will not be basing ourselves much on that document in any case. So the question of admitting it or not admitting it may, in effect, assume secondary importance in most instances. So this is what I wanted to make clear. And if I have again not made myself clear, please let us know and we will make it clearer hopefully and shorter too. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's very helpful, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Agreed facts. Now, this is where, for the present moment, I will be very short. You know that there is the possibility for you to agree and come forward with a number of facts on which you agree and which can be taken as adjudicated facts. But there is also the option that this Trial Chamber has, having gone through documentation, to decide itself to admit certain evidence as adjudicated facts. I can assure you that in doing so, the Trial Chamber will observe the basic principle underlying the rule which governs this procedural measure. But the Trial Chamber as such, before even thinking of proceeding along these lines, would exhort you to try, seriously try to meet when there is time, possibly also with the help of our Senior Legal Officer, and try to at least identify various facts on which there should be no reason for you to disagree about. I will not give instances so that no one will accuse the Trial Chamber of having expressed itself on any particular fact. But I was, in the course of last week, for example, reading the decision in the Kvocka case, which to a large extent, deals with some of the camps, with Omarska, very little with Trnopolje and Keraterm, but it deals to a large extent with Omarska and what took place then. You realise, I mean I don't need to say much on this, that what happened in Omarska is one thing and if the Defence, for example, contests that those facts ever happened in those camps, then I will shut up immediately. But if, for the Defence, what is important is the nexus or the absence of it, which would establish or rule out the responsibility of each of the two accused with those events, then I'm suggesting to you that it may well be the case that you sit down together, because if the Defence is going to be on the side of Mr. Brdjanin, "I never knew that those events were happening there. I had nothing to do with those events, I had no control on what was happening there, there was no time during which I could have acted positively or negatively," the same line of Defence is brought forward on behalf of General Talic, then we should concentrate on that line of the Defence and not on whether the events that were found to have taken place in the Kvocka case, whether they have happened or not. My suggestion to you is to see whether it is at all possible for the two sides, when I say two sides, General Talic, Mr. Brdjanin, and Prosecution, to identify areas where there are facts that you need not contest or that you have no intention of contesting. There will absolutely be no further invitation on the part of the Trial Chamber to reach such an agreement with regard to any particular event. This is up to you. But I am putting it to you that the more I read, the more I am convincing myself that there may come a time when this Trial Chamber will necessarily have to put its foot down and admit in evidence as adjudicated facts, certain facts arising from other events. That is a possibility which this Tribunal will try to avoid if necessary but there are certainly many facts on which it would be reasonable for this Trial Chamber to expect you to reach an agreement upon. This is an exercise that I would like you to -- I know that there has been this approach already from the Prosecution et cetera and I have also told my Senior Legal Officer that if the Defence is expected to come forward and cooperate in this, the Prosecution needs to present a completely different and new list of facts on which it seeks your agreement. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a few things I need to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. advise the Chamber with regard to this issue. I take what you're saying very seriously and have since the beginning of the case. The first thing that the Chamber must understand is that for either one of us to provide you with a list of facts that we agree to is of no value unless both of us do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that's the first thing that has to be dealt with. The second thing I will tell you in that regard is that the issue of the representation of General Talic is one that has been in flux since the beginning of this case and is obviously going to be that way until at least the 20th when General Talic told you this morning he would advise you as to whether Mr. De Roux will be remaining as his lead counsel or not. Until we have a complete General Talic Defence team, it's extraordinarily difficult for me to sit down with the Talic Defence and arrive at any kind of agreements in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, I'll say to you it's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't expecting this to happen between today and tomorrow or the end of the week. Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I would like you to understand is that we are cognizant of it and we are working on it and it is something we all have in mind. No one has any desire to prolong this trial by requiring unnecessary proof of facts. It will also be of absolutely no value at this point or perhaps any time in the future for us to have some kind of meeting with the Prosecutor because we know what the facts are that are alleged by the Prosecutor and we are perfectly capable, the two Defence teams, I hope, of sitting down and saying we should go along with some of these. Now, one thing that I might ask the Chamber to consider, which might make this an easier process, rather than for us to say to the Trial Chamber, "We admit this certain sets of facts," is if we could be permitted to say to the Trial Chamber that we do not contest this particular set of facts. It's one thing to say we admit all the facts alleged with regard to what happened in the camp at Omarska and another thing to say we simply do not contest them. That is an issue that I don't know has ever been before a Trial Chamber in this Tribunal. It's fairly common where I come from. You can even enter a plea of nolo contendere, which means you're not making any kind of admission and where it might be very difficult to make an admission of facts, it's quite easy to do to simply say, "I do not contest these facts for the purposes of this trial" and it seems to me that accomplishes the same thing. It takes the Prosecutor off the hook in terms of having to prove them. So I'd like you to consider whether you would accept that kind of an agreement, representation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will obviously discuss it amongst ourselves because we were not exactly expecting -- we didn't know what you were going to -- what your response was going to be. But I think I will -- I do not anticipate problems. Certainly, I can assure you of something that this Trial Chamber is very clear about, or hasn't got any doubts about. That is that the fact that you may either be requested, called upon, or voluntarily come forward and say, "We do not contest these facts," will not at any time then or afterwards be taken to mean, first, that your clients knew that those events were taking place or that they personally accept the fact that they are being not contested to be in any way used against them or to be prejudicial to them. In other words, that is something that we want to make clear to you, that if you say, "We do not contest that the conditions, the hygienic conditions in Omarska camp were really bad. Secondly that the food was very bad, that persons were tortured, and beaten up and summarily executed in Omarska. We do not contest that that happened," doesn't mean to say that they are agreeing that they knew about those events at the time they were happening or that they had some -- or some sort of control over the situation. The agreement or the non-contestation of those events would be of course without prejudice to their guilt or otherwise. This is pretty obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you have just identified the major problem, and that is how can one admit that something occurred if they have no idea whether it did or not. And that's why I'm trying to suggest that we could do a no contest kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a no contest, exactly. I'm not saying that you will enter a declaration to the effect that you agree that those events happened. That you do not contest that those events happened. Which would dispense the Prosecution from the need to bring forward the witnesses in persona, unless the Prosecution has reason to believe that apart from giving evidence on the happening of those events proper, those witnesses will also give information relating -- related to the responsibility, personal responsibility, of one or both of the accused. But I think this is something that we can discuss further as we go along, but please do keep it in mind as we move ahead and as we approach the phase of hearing evidence on these events. I have several reasons why I'm bringing this up. These are -- if these events happened, and there are decisions of this Tribunal stating that these events happened, I would imagine that the same persons that gave evidence in the previous trials are going to be brought forward again into this -- into The Hague, into this courtroom, to give evidence again on these events, which you, Mr. Ackerman, I'm sure, have heard before, and if you haven't heard in a courtroom, you have read, like I have, and if we can avoid a repetition of that, in other words if we can avoid having these persons come again here and go through what I would consider as an ordeal to them and to us, if we can avoid it, I would appeal to positive approach. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We just -- I keep thinking of problems. And I'm sorry. The other problem that I see we are talking about Omarska right now and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned Omarska because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- that involves Prijedor and I know there is going to be an attempt to coordinate the evidence in the Stakic case and this case with regard to Prijedor and I can just see that while the two of us here may be saying, "You don't need to call witnesses A, B, C, but only D," the Stakic Defence will be saying, "You have to call all of them," and in then what do we do in the meantime while we're waiting for the next witness to come? I'm not sure that coordination is going to work at all but I'm certainly willing to watch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it like this, Mr. Ackerman: That may well happen with regard to the Prijedor chapter, but the Prijedor chapter is not the only one that we have. There are many events that have been dealt with in at least three or four other cases that are common to this trial as well, which we can -- I don't know. But it's, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It really is only Prijedor. None the of the other municipalities that we are calling evidence, at least that I can think of offhand, there has been no trials about any of them. Prijedor has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Only Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Really only Prijedor is about -- other than there are of course other trials but they have dealt with perhaps Bosnia and within this area only Prijedor has been litigated. That's the only one really to which it applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Even with the others, Your Honour there may be facts alleged with regard to those municipalities that we would not be interested in contesting whether there has been prior trials about them or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but as soon as the Defence of General Talic problem, in inverted commas, crystallises, I suppose I have told you what I have in mind and more or less you know what I'm -- which lines I'm thinking along, and perhaps you could in the meantime see what could be done by way of trying to reduce the need to have certain evidence be brought forward. If that can be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour will have seen from the meeting, at page 23, that I foresaw that this was a problem, about the question of making admissions, and we dealt with, as Mr. Ackerman suggests, nolo, contendere, not disputed, or whatever the expression is. What we propose do when we come to the next municipality, Sanski Most, is produce a short list of facts which we would hope would not be in dispute. For example, that there were prison camps at the following places, that they cannot dispute that ill treatment took place and so on and so forth. And see where that gets us. We would, of course, hope to reduce the witnesses thereby, but most of the witnesses are being called that specifically refer to matters on the indictment. So we would have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the reason why we haven't reacted as yet, and that we have left all doors open for the Prosecution without interfering at all with any of the witnesses that you have declared so far. The reason is that we realise that this is not an easy case, this is a complicated case, which will take a long time, and we will only, not interfere but we will only become proactive in that direction when we see that you're not being reasonable. But not being reasonable in insisting and bringing forward a witness to repeat the same thing, the same fact, over and over again. Then we will stop you. But until then, we will not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's why we have selected a number of witnesses for the Rule 92 procedure to try and cut down on that very thing. Your Honour, there are five or so municipalities which have more events than others. Some of them are smaller and shorter and more compact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. So that deals -- then there was an another chapter which was opened during that meeting which is interesting. And that is the length of the trial. More or less we just touched upon it now as well. Here it says the Prosecution expressed some concern about whether the Trial Chamber would at some future point impose a strict time limit on them for the completion of the case. This has recently been done in a particular case that you mention here, if so the Prosecution seeks adequate warning so that they have a realistic possibility of apportioning the remainder of that case in a balanced way. Now, I will tell you very little here but you will have seen the way the Trial Chamber proceeded while Mr. Krzic was giving evidence. We are definitely not short of patience. This Trial Chamber is very patient. And this Trial Chamber, therefore, will most probably never have -- feel to have to resort to the measure that has been resorted to in another case. Unless there is reason to make us change our minds. But so far, as things are going, we think that we have no criticism to raise both in regard to the way you have conducted your examination-in-chiefs or to the way that the Defence have behaved in -- during the trial and also in the course of the cross-examinations. So if that is the case, you will have all the space and all the facilities necessary for you to conclude your case as you think you require. The same applies to the Defence. I me, we are acting under the conviction that we all mean business and that we are constructive in our approach. In other words I have no reason to doubt that you have every intention to get this case over and done with, the sooner the better, and similarly, I have no reason to doubt about the good intentions of the Defence now that the trial has started. I mean, it's a difficult trial for all of us and I think there is a spirit of cooperation in the air which we don't have a reason to doubt so far and therefore don't expect for the moment any sort of measures to be taken. If the situation, the position, changes, then obviously you are going to be given ample time, forewarning, I don't think there should be reason for you to have any doubts on that or to face -- to fear that you would find yourself faced with an emergency that would be created for you by the Trial Chamber itself. It's in not our style and we won't do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I just mention, Your Honour, in respect -- and we are grateful to Your Honour for that indication, Your Honours remarks in respect of Mr. Krzic, experience has taught all of us who have dealt with witnesses from Bosnia that there is a tendency to not exactly answer the question that was asked or to answer it but with a long explanation. All witnesses are warned by us in advance only to answer the questions they are asked, but obviously it's more difficult when they are in court. But it may help, I think if Your Honour, with the presence that Your Honours have, before a witness starts, just remind them that if they stick to answering the question they are asked, they will be out of here quicker or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will try to deal with each witness case by case, because there are some witnesses where this kind of practice simply -- not simply doesn't work but they almost take offence sometimes. They think that there is an attempt on the part of, if not -- if it's forthcoming from the trial Chamber itself, from the Trial Chamber, from the Tribunal. Sometimes it's more dangerous if it's coming from either you or from the Defence, because they react to it and it may lengthen rather than shorten the testimony. So I understand and I fully agree that we should do something about it as we go along. But please do understand also that it varies from witness to witness. There are witnesses who are more prone to cooperate than others. Okay? Each witness comes forward, it happens in my jurisdiction as well, in Malta, they want to tell you the story of their life and we have to bring them to order but sometimes especially if they are persons that have gone through a lot, we have to be extremely careful not to make things worse because we may have a reaction that you wouldn't anticipate or you wouldn't like to have in the courtroom. So I also would like your cooperation in this, but be careful, especially, for example, I would prefer if you, Mr. Ackerman, draws my attention that perhaps I should bring the witness to order rather than doing it yourself, because he may take objection when -- to you, knowing who you are and who you represent, but he or she would not take that much objection if we intervene. Okay. So that settles that. There was also a strong recommendation that was made to us by our Senior Legal Officer, that before the trial moves on to any new municipality, the Trial Chamber will make an assessment of the Prosecution's case in some depth. Consequently in preparing for the next premunicipality meeting, an analysis would be carried out based on one, the outline of evidence that has already been presented in the case. Two, the way the witnesses proposed for the upcoming municipality would fit with that outline of evidence. Three, the way proposed Rule 92 bis statements would fit with that outline of evidence. Four, the way that facts already determined in other cases, this is where I put a lot of emphasis, on appeal and not related directly to the accused, may fit in with that outline of evidence, such facts may be considered as adjudicated facts, either on the basis of a submission from the Prosecution or by the Trial Chamber proprio motu. Next the way suggested exhibits from the upcoming municipality may fit in with the outline of evidence and last but not least, the way facts agreed upon between the parties may fit in with that outline of evidence. I think without having heard a reaction from the interpreters, that I have been reading a little bit too fast. So I think I will give them a chance to finish the interpretation before I say something else. And I apologise to them. These are I think good suggestions. I understand that these were more or less aired during the discussion that is you had, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was about to say thank you very much to Mr. Von Hebel because that's the first we heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was a slight touching on agreed facts, but that's about it. We'd like time to consider obviously what Your Honour is requiring here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. If you want, I can let you have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I have just done, Ms. Korner, is since this is a more or less a confidential report that the Senior Legal Officer prepared for us, what I'm suggesting is that we extract the relative paragraphs which is what I have just read plus another recommendation, which runs as follows: Consequently, one or two weeks before the premunicipality meeting, the Prosecution would be requested, here it says "would have to," would be invited to - we use moderate terms - submit the statements of the witnesses. That's for the purposes that you all know of. And the 92 bis statements. And that would incorporate and be prepared also to provide tape recordings. And the list of facts that they-- that they think could be agreed upon. Again we will discuss this, taking into consideration what was mentioned by Mr. Ackerman, that they would rather prefer not to be provided with such lists from the Prosecution, they are capable enough of coming forward themselves with a list of facts that they would decide not to contest. And then it continues on the basis of this material the Trial Chamber would carry out a detailed analysis. This could then lead to further instructions to the Prosecution as to how to organise or limit the evidence that they would like to submit. This would be done in a manner that avoids presenting any preliminary views on the evidence and gives the Prosecution adequate flexibility in the presentation of its case. What I would like to assure you of is that we will definitely give you, afford you, all the flexibility needed and the space required, not just to you, Madam Prosecutor, but also to the Defence teams in the preparation of your cases. As we go along, what my appeal to you is, is let's talk, let's sit down around a table and see how we can make this case run smoother. This is important. Okay? So -- and I agree that we shouldn't leave it until the very last moment when the next meeting will be held prior to the next municipality. We should start working on preparing for that meeting well in advance. This is what I -- preparing on your side and also on your side. You will be of course in a position to know which facts you would agree to, if you are provided with the facts beforehand. So this is why it is necessary that you start working on this in good time. Or in real time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I understand correctly, it's the try Chamber that is going to do the analysis and not us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Analysis of what is needed to streamline, then, the proceedings for the next municipality. For example, I won't be saying, telling any secrets but before this trial started, our legal staff prepared for us a breakdown of all the evidence that you intend to bring forward, number-wise and volume-wise with regard to several items or points or events as they emerge from the indictment itself. For example, I don't know, the breakdown of the Communist Party in 1990 or 1991, how many witnesses you intended to bring forward, more or less the same exercise will -- our staff will be doing that exercise for us as we go along. It doesn't mean to say that we are deciding or analysing what the case for the Prosecution will be like, but more or less on the basis of what we are told by the -- by our team, we would be in a better position to direct you. In other words, we will possibly ask you, listen Ms. Korner with regard to this particular event, you're intending to bring forward 23 witnesses. Could you possibly tell us whether all the 23 are needed or whether it's the case of going through them yourselves and possibly finding out whether we can live with 16 or 18 or whether for each municipality, for example, we is should limit them to 15 or 20, unless there is absolute need to have more, I don't know. We will be working, what I promise you is we will try to find ways and means of working hand in hand with you. Okay? This is the approach that will be taken by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Your Honour will find that that never happens, because there were so many incidents, there is only effectively one witness and maybe one Rule 92 for each incident in the major municipalities. The only reason actually I'm on my feet is to say do I understand that Your Honour would like in advance not as we originally suggested, that you would have the statement of the witness that was coming a few days or a week, but the whole bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm less interested, Ms. Korner, in myself and the other two judges having those documents much ahead time. It would be helpful if we have them well ahead in time, because we will be in a better position to form a general bird's-eye-view of what evidence you intend to bring forward and how your case is likely to present itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can provide each of Your Honours with a bundle of all the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's more important, and I'm sure you understand me now that we are getting to know each other better, it's more important for me to know that the Defence have that material in hand because then I can look towards Mr. Ackerman and towards Madam Fauveau and say, "You have had ample time to go through these. Can I ask you whether there are facts to which you are prepared to say, we do not contest that these facts may have happened?"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the list for Sanski Most will be given to the Defence this week. They have all the statements already but the order in which we intend to call them. There is one query which I raise simply now from the point of view of witness management. On our rough and ready estimate, although I think it's already been thrown out slightly, we estimated that we would finish the Banja Luka municipality by the -- somewhere in the beginning of the week before the week we -- that ends on the 22nd of March but we worked out there would be two days, that is to say the 20th and 21st where we could start Sanski Most so I only raise it now for consideration whether you and the Defence would wish to start the Sanski Most in those last or wait until after the Easter break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, we would continue, start straight away with Sanski Most. There is no reason why we should stop. If the necessary documentation is readily available, we should straight away with Sanski Most. Do you have an objection to that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I might present the Chamber with a bundle of the emails from my wife that are starting to build regarding that I'm not being given an opportunity to come back to Texas, and also from the problems that are going on in my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will not change the dates we have agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But an additional couple of days would sure be helpful. I don't think we will finish by then but if we did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have not thought of blocking your wife's email?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then I would have to find another wife, I suppose, Judge and I really like the one I have a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My wife has asked me to teach her email and I said, when I have time. When this trial leaves me time. Yes, we will -- any way, we will play it by the ear because it may well be that after all, we will get, we will encounter some problems which would not make it possible for us to proceed with Sanski Most in those two days and we could also find ourselves not being able of -- to finish the Banja Luka. Anything could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just -- I don't want to miss the opportunity, Your Honour, to strongly suggest that after the March 22nd break, that we get on some kind after schedule with fairly frequent, one-week breaks. The -- none of us who have agreed to become involved in cases here at this Tribunal have agreed to completely close our law practices in order to be able to do business here. And those of us who come from western countries are working for half or less of what we charge for work that we do at home. So we see our efforts here as being to some extent pro bono and I certainly see my efforts here as being, to some extent, pro bono and I should not have to completely lose my law practice to engage in pro bono work for this Tribunal. It's a work that I love. It's a work that I like doing and it's a work that I want to continue doing, but if I have to be here straight through months and months of trial, I simply will not be able to do it. I can't. And so I hope that the Chamber will consider that we go on a schedule similar to what I suggested and you indicated, Your Honour, that you thought might be acceptable and that is a four weeks of trial with a week off. That would work for me. I think it would work for all of us who might need to try to keep other work and keep our offices together and our lives together and everything else. I understand it's important that we move forward but it's also important that we do it reasonably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has already expressed itself on this in the beginning of this trial, or even before this trial started. I -- what I would suggest is that you try to work out, to discuss amongst yourselves, the two Defence teams, together with the Prosecution, because you will understand that it's not fair, while the Prosecution, for example, is dealing with one municipality, for this Trial Chamber to say, "Now you will stop for two weeks or one week or three weeks. We will continue afterwards." I would -- definitely we promised you that we will definitely meet you not halfway, even beyond that, in staggering the weeks when there will be hearings and the weeks when there will be a break. That will happen. There is no question. But it could well be, for example, that there will be -- it will be needed to have a break, say, after two weeks rather than four or five weeks rather than four. This is why I'm telling you try and work out together with the Prosecution -- try -- I mean everyone needs to be accommodated. In other words, you ought to keep in mind also the programme or the chapter that the Prosecution would be dealing with and the importance not to have evidence being brought forward in bits and pieces. I think you know what I mean. You have been a lawyer for a long number of years. It is important sometimes to follow the train and the momentum of bringing forward one witness over -- after another, for fear of certain things happening in the meantime. So more or less, I would like to have a feedback also from the Prosecution in this regard, and I would rather prefer that you plan it for the Trial Chamber beforehand rather than discuss it or make an issue out of it here. I think you have cooperated already, I mean that's the impression that we have. That there shouldn't be -- there is no bad blood between you or a polluted environment in which you cannot sit down together and agree on this. And the Trial Chamber will come not meet you halfway we will definitely meet you all the way in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour we will certainly discuss matters. It's just been brought to my attention in fact by Ms. Richterova that there may be a problem starting immediately the Tuesday after Easter because of the holidays and trying to get witnesses here to begin on the Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Holidays in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will -- I will discuss this matter and we'll get back to Your Honour on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will find that we will -- you don't have -- you shouldn't have any reason to believe for a moment that we will not cooperate with you. I fully understand that no lawyer should be expected to give up his practice. You don't even need to remind me of that. On the other hand, I mean, rather than telling me we need to break one week every four weeks, sit down with Ms. Korner, tell me that between now and June, this is how we would like to work. Keeping in mind also that there is more than one eye cast and focused on how trials are being conducted and how expeditiously trials are being conducted or how much -- how many Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. breaks are being taken et cetera. This is all being monitored and I am sure you appreciate that the intention of whoever is responsible for this Tribunal as well as the one in Arusha, is that the least time possible is wasted and the time available is used to have trials heard and determined as expeditiously and as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I appreciate very much what you've said, Your Honour, and let me just tell you a couple more things. I was in, as you know, the Celebici trial, and because of the fact that we only had one court room and two trials going on, we were sharing a courtroom with the Blaskic case and they would have it for two weeks and then we would have it for two weeks. And that certainly meant that the Prosecution was not able to really finish a segment in two weeks, that it was going -- and it didn't really affect the flow of the Prosecution's case in any significant way, I can tell you that. The other thing that we learned in that process was that during those two week breaks in that case, an enormous amount of work was done by counsel so that the following two weeks was a great deal more productive than it otherwise would have been so I think that case moved almost as fast as it would have had we been in session every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have no doubt that it will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I don't think anyone watching from the outside should think that we are just going on vacation every now and then because we are not. We continue to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have worked here and you know what you're talking about and I have worked as a Judge for 25 years and I know what I'm talking about. But I am not going to surprise you that many people outside will still believe that when the Judge here and everywhere else leaves his Chamber at, I don't know what time, that's the end of the day's work for him. And it's wrong. Or that if you have a week off, then you are going to be on holiday for that week, as Defence counsel or as Prosecutor. It's wrong, but we know it's wrong, not many people don't. Many people would still think that you and I and everyone else are just having a good time or want to have a good time when we take a week or two weeks off which is not the case. I know. It's very important for the cases to be interrupted periodically so that each side reorganises the team and the case and you will of course be afforded all the possibility. I mean it would be very unfair for this Trial Chamber not to interrupt periodically the sequence of sittings because it would deprive you of the best way possible to reorganise your own teams and your own fronts so that is enough. But what I meant was please sit down together and in the most flexible way come forward and let us know what you would like. Then be also prepared to be flexible later on if the needs arise to change the schedule, because it may well be that we will need to change the schedule as we need it when we first fixed the March 22 break, you told me that Mr. Brdjanin's wife will be coming over, she had already from such and such a date to such and such a day. You have to be flexible. We will be flexible and you have to be flexible. So that more or less concludes what I needed to tell you. You will have a copy of an a extract of the report from Mr. Von Hebel and I would appreciate if you could give us a feedback. There are two options. You could give us a feedback directly to the Trial Chamber or you could, and I would rather prefer this to happen this way, you could give a feedback to Mr. Von Hebel himself, who may then discuss it further with you, or elaborate a scheme whereby the preparation for the next informal municipal Status Conference or meeting will be held, so that we would be working along the same lines and would be fine-tuned with one another. So that is the position. Now, it's 10 past 12.00. Is there anything else that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we start with the witness? At least we will give him good half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Richterova is going to start the witness. Do you I understand Your Honour wishes to rise at quarter to 1.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, we will keep an eye on the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness is 7.87, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you call and bring in witness -- I think he has gone for him already. Okay. This witness, has he asked for protective measures? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm addressing you, sir. Can you look at me, please? Are you understanding me in a language -- or are you hearing me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you and I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the gentleman to your right will give you a document which contains a solemn declaration that you are being requested to make, a declaration that you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. And you are kindly asked to make that solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down, sir, thank you. Just before you start, before you start, I am the Presiding Judge in this trial and I am flanked by two other judges that will be hearing and deciding this case. To your right, there is the team for the Prosecution, lawyers for the Prosecution. And the lady standing up will very soon start asking, putting questions to you and to your left you have two teams for the Defence. The front row and then the back. The team in the front row is counsel for defendant Brdjanin, Radoslav Brdjanin, while the lady in the back is counsel for General Talic. Persons in front here are the -- form part of the Registry. You are now going to be asked a series of questions. They will be asked in English, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There will be simultaneous translation into a language that you understand. If at any time the simultaneous translation is not forthcoming is not reaching you, please make me a signal, give me a sign, and we will wait until you receive a proper translation. One very important thing, sir, is that if you do not take my advice, you will be here for days and days and days and you will get tired and we will get tired. You will be asked questions. Here you will be required to answer that question, the whole question and nothing but that question. The Tribunal is not interested in hearing anything else. Don't tell us stories that you are not asked about. We are not interested in your childhood, in the events of your life, other than the ones that you will be asked upon. Have I made myself understood, clearly understood to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now the lady counsel for Prosecution will be commencing her examination-in-chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, I would say good afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: My name is Zijahudin Smailagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell us the date and the place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: I was born in Banja Luka on the 10th of December, 1940.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What is your nationality and what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Islam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges where did you live in the period 1990 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: I lived in Banja Luka in my house in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show you a map. We have unfortunately only one copy. I know it's not a happy start of my appearance that I am not ready, but we will have sufficient amount of maps within one hour, if not within one hour, tomorrow morning, but I would like to state that this similar map was already exhibited under P2, and the exhibit under P2 was annotated by Mr. Mazhar. This is blown up version of very similar map and it would be easier for the witness to orient on this map. Can we place it, please, on the ELMO? I would like to exhibit this map when you have the spare copies, as P2.1A, just P2.1, because it will be only one version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That map is being admitted. And will be marked as indicated by counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, can you indicate on the map the part of the town where you lived in the period which I stated? You have the map next to you, so you can indicate on the map. Take your time and -- no you have to do it on the real map.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: This part which is called Pobrdje. It's in the town itself. It's a neighbourhood called Pobrdje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, so may I ask the registrar to give you a pen, preferably coloured red, and ask you to mark on that map by means of a circle the point you are indicating to us now, and then initial, put your initials next to the mark.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was typical ethnic structure of population for this particular area?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: 90 per cent of the population in Pobrdje was Muslim. They were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said this was one part of the town, Banja Luka. Were there other separate parts within Banja Luka town?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were other parts. To the left and to the right, Novo Selija, Gornji Seher, Mejdan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Would you assist us and explain what was ethnic structure of population of these separate parts in the town?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Left and right Novo Selija and Gornji Seher there was a predominantly Muslim population here, perhaps even of 80 per cent of the population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I stop you for a moment? Would you be so kind and point on your map the places which you are talking about? Take your time and show us the places you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And mark, as you go along, Mr. Smailagic, as you go along, please mark with a "X" this time, with a "X" on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Hiseta neighbourhood, which extends towards Gornji Seher and Novo Selija and the population here is mainly Muslim, that is to say they are Bosniaks. Just a minute. This is the Mejdan neighbourhood. The population here was also -- there were quite a lot of Muslims here. It was a mixed neighbourhood. I can't see here. I can't see Gornji Seher here and Novo Selija, so I can't mark them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the ethnic structure in these two areas?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Mainly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what was the ethnic structure of the Banja Luka municipality, if you could explain the differences between the town villages, if there were any?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka, you are referring to the town, the town of Banja Luka, the population was mainly Muslim in that town, but as a municipality, when we are talking about Banja Luka municipality, the Serbian -- the Serbians were in the majority. As a municipality, Banja Luka, Krupa and Vrbas was not in the Banja Luka municipality, nor was Mejdan and Prozor but part of the municipality of Banja Luka was Celinac and Laktasi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what was the existing ethnic structure of Celinac and Laktasi at that time when it was part of Banja Luka municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: It was mixed in Celinac, there were quite a few Muslims and case was the same in Laktasi. And there was a village called Mahovljani too in which the population was mainly Muslim and these municipalities were part of the organisation -- of the municipality of Banja Luka. They were separated but they joined the municipality of Krupa na Vrbas, Bronzon and Mejdan. There was also the Ivanjska municipality, which joined Banja Luka. Krupa na Vrbas is about 45 kilometres from Banja Luka. Bronzon and Mejdan are about 32 or 34 kilometres from Banja Luka, whereas Celinac is about 15 kilometres from Banja Luka and it is kept apart from Banja Luka municipality. Laktasi is 19 kilometres from Banja Luka and is separate from bang Banja Luka. This was done in my opinion in order to change the demographic structure of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move from this subject and I would like to ask you, you said that there were these separate parts of the town. How they were organised, into which structures?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Referring to Celinac and Laktasi?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. I mean you mentioned you live in Pobrdje which was separate part of the town. How did you -- did you call this separate part in some way? I think I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can ask him a direct question. I mean there's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think I can help you. I'm asking about these self-governing areas which you called local community. Local communes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have permission to use even the local word, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered the question. I mean I haven't heard an answer at least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The majority of the population in Pobrdje, which is where I lived, the majority was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How was it organised? Were there some authorities in these local communes?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: They were -- organs were elected in the local commune. There was a municipal assembly and it had its own executive committee which implemented tasks which were given to it by the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, I would like to move from this subject and -- but we will return to municipal, local commune assembly and other authorities. I want to ask you about your involvement in politics, beginning 1990. Were you a member of some political party before 1990 and after 1990?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Before 1990, I wasn't a member of any party, and I didn't participate in politics in any way. In the 1990s, I became a member of the Party of Democratic Action, and since then, I remained an active member in that party, in the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you hold any position in -- within the party of SDA?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: After the elections, I was elected as the Vice-President of a branch of the party for the local commune of Pobrdje, and my function, according to the programme of the party, the Vice-President were immediately members of the main committee of the party for Banja Luka. So as the Vice-President in the branch of the local commune for the Party of Democratic Action and a member of the main committee for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where were located premises of this main board of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the Party of Democratic Action were in the Dom Kultura, the Culture Club, on the first floor of this building, and it is now called the Banski Nori [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richterova. I know that you speak the same language as the witness does, so you know the answer before we get the translation. The interpreters are having a little bit of a problem. Between his finishing his answer and you putting the next question, please give it a little bit of time so that they finish the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I do the same mistake all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there some other parties within the premises in Dom Kultura?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Party of Democratic Action was there, the Serbian Democratic Party, and the Croatian Democratic Community.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you mention Party of Democratic Action, what was the ethnic composition of members after this party was established?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: With the formation of the Party of Democratic Action in the 1990s, it was multi-national at the time. We formed before the HDZ so that part of -- some Croats joined our party, and there were also some Serbs, to tell you the truth. They were members for a certain time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did it change at some point, the structure of your party?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. With the formation of the HDZ, these gentlemen left and moved to the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you -- did you hold some responsibility also within local community? Did you receive some -- did you have some functions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can ask him a direct question here, because these are facts that are not going to be contested in any case, I mean whether he had a -- just put the question straight to him. You know whether he did or he didn't. And if there is an objection forthcoming from the Prosecution, we will change course. But in the meantime, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour meant the Defence. I'm not going to object to Ms. Richterova's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From the Defence, yes, from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you president of the local community assembly in Pobrdje?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the multi-party elections which were held in the 1990s, there were elections in the local communes which were held too, and I was elected as the president of the local commune assembly in the local commune of Pobrdje.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to really very briefly ask something what we have already mentioned at the beginning but I would like to mention it here again. After 1990, were there some initials -- initiatives to change the structure of the Banja Luka municipality? Were there some initiatives to change -- to divide municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That idea was present before the -- before 1990. There was a forum of intellectuals in Banja Luka which was responsible for this idea, and there was an expert -- a team of experts, well-known Banja Luka intellectuals formed it, and it was headed by Dr. Sabahudin Osmancevic. There was a restructuring of the Banja Luka municipality, and it was divided into nine smaller municipalities so that Banja Luka as a town would be a separate municipality, but account was taken of the national composition, to ensure that it was fairly mixed so that weight could be taken off the town and in order to satisfy all needs. And this required the support, unconditional support, of all three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was this idea supported also by all three parties?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: That idea was present even before the formation of the party, before the multi-party elections. It was reanimated after the multi-party elections, and in some conversations, yes, there was support on the part of all three parties. But when the plan was sent for adoption to the assembly, then the representatives of the SDS parties were energetic and didn't allow it. We then sent it to the republican parliament, but it was never dealt with. Then there was the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you a few questions about the life of parties. Were there any interparty meetings, I mean meetings among HDZ, SDA, SDS, during 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were joint meetings. At the beginning, there was certain attempts at reaching agreements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where were these meetings take place -- took place?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC
utterances.text: They took place in the Dom Kultura. There were common premises on the same floor. And sometimes they were on the premises of the HDZ; sometimes in the premises of the Serbian Democratic Party; and sometimes in our premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we stop here?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We can stop here because then I have a series of questions which I think we need much more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, we have to stop here for today. Tomorrow we will continue. I thank you for your patience and your cooperation. So we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. We will try to make up for the time we have [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just make one thing clear? This witness is staying in the same hotel as the following witness. There is a limited number of hotels in The Hague in which they can be put. I understand that both certainly have been instructed by myself and Ms. Richterova not to speak to each other about the evidence they are giving, but I think it's only fair that we should let the Defence know and perhaps Mr. Smailagic could be give that warning reinforced by Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he know who the other witness is?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He does, Your Honour. They know each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They know each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other witness hasn't asked for any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, he hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can mention the name?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, I understand -- you have heard what the Prosecutor has just stated, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Didn't have the earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let me explain to you. I have just been informed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Staying in the same hotel that you are staying in, there is another Bosniak who will be giving evidence after you. I'm referring to Amir Dzonlic. You know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, you must give me your word that while you are here in The Hague, and until you have finished giving evidence, you will under no circumstance discuss any matter related to this case, to your evidence, or to the events surrounding this particular case and the events that happened in your country with the next witness, Mr. Dzonlic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I promise that I shall behave in such a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you also promise that you will not allow Mr. Dzonlic, who is not here to receive such a warning, not to speak to you about these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also promise to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't need to explain to you the importance of this, but if this advice is not heeded, one of the most obvious consequences will be that no one will believe you, apart from other considerations. And I take your word as a gentleman that you will heed my advice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that satisfy you, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm most grateful to Your Honour, and Mr. Dzonlic was in fact given that warning yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not here so -- we'll meet tomorrow morning at 9.00. I thank you. And Mr. Smailagic tomorrow will continue his giving -- being examined in chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
